traditions.name: Laissez-faire capitalism
traditions.description: private ownership, minimal state (defense, courts, contract enforcement).
overview: Laissez-faire capitalism is a family of arguments for organizing most production and exchange through private property, voluntary contract, market prices, and competition. In its minimal-state forms, public authority still defines and enforces property, contract, and protections against force or fraud.

The tradition places unusual confidence in decentralized choice and price signals, while treating concentrated public discretion as a recurring danger. Its central disputes concern whether nominally voluntary exchange remains meaningfully voluntary when wealth, bargaining power, information, or market access are highly unequal.
distinctions: Minimal-state capitalism, not the absence of all government
A theoretical tradition, not a description of every market economy
Private ownership and contract as institutions that still require rules and enforcement

commonQuestions.question: Is laissez-faire capitalism the same as anarcho-capitalism?
commonQuestions.answer: No. Most laissez-faire traditions retain a state for courts, defense, property, and contract enforcement. Anarcho-capitalism proposes private provision of those functions as well.

commonQuestions.question: Does laissez-faire mean that markets have no rules?
commonQuestions.answer: No. Property, contract, liability, bankruptcy, and corporate forms are rules. The disagreement is mainly about their scope, source, and how much discretionary regulation should accompany them.

commonQuestions.question: Has a completely laissez-faire economy existed?
commonQuestions.answer: That is not established here. Historical economies combine public and private institutions, so the label is better used for a direction of argument or an ideal type than as an unqualified country classification.

traditions.caveat: Exploratory ideal-type description. It does not identify a country, case, advocate, or internally uniform tradition.

traditions.name: Social-democratic capitalism
traditions.description: private ownership and markets plus a large tax-funded state correcting failures and redistributing. Nordic model; the German variant adds codetermination.
overview: Social-democratic capitalism combines predominantly private ownership and market coordination with democratic government, collective bargaining, social insurance, public services, and economic regulation. It generally seeks to constrain the risks and inequalities of capitalism without replacing markets as the main coordinating institution.

There is no single social-democratic package. Nordic, continental European, and later reform traditions differ over ownership, unions, taxation, industrial policy, universal benefits, and the degree to which workers should share authority inside firms.
distinctions: Capitalist ownership with extensive social and democratic constraints
Broader than a welfare state alone
Historically variable across parties, countries, and periods

commonQuestions.question: Is social democracy the same as democratic socialism?
commonQuestions.answer: They overlap historically and politically, but they are not interchangeable. Many contemporary social democrats accept a durable mixed capitalist economy, while democratic socialists generally seek deeper changes in ownership or economic authority.

commonQuestions.question: Does social democracy mean that the state runs most businesses?
commonQuestions.answer: Not necessarily. Its characteristic arrangements can include private firms, public enterprises, cooperatives, regulated markets, collective bargaining, and tax-funded services in different combinations.

commonQuestions.question: Is the Nordic model one uniform system?
commonQuestions.answer: No. Nordic institutions differ by country and have changed substantially over time. The phrase is a comparative shorthand, not a complete institutional description.

traditions.caveat: Exploratory ideal-type description. It does not identify a country, case, advocate, or internally uniform tradition.

traditions.name: Market socialism / economic democracy
traditions.description: worker-managed or socially-owned firms competing in markets. Schweickart's model, Yugoslav self-management, Mondragón-style cooperative federations.
overview: Market socialism and economic democracy describe proposals that retain markets for at least some allocation while changing who owns firms, who governs workplaces, or who receives returns to capital. Common models emphasize worker cooperatives, social investment funds, public ownership, or combinations of these institutions.

The category contains major disagreements. Some approaches center workplace democracy, others social ownership of investment, and others a mixed economy with stronger worker voice. Their shared question is whether market coordination can be separated from concentrated private ownership and hierarchical control.
distinctions: Markets without conventional capital ownership as the defining combination
Not one blueprint for cooperatives or public ownership
Workplace authority and investment control are separate design questions

commonQuestions.question: Is market socialism a contradiction?
commonQuestions.answer: Not by definition. Markets describe a mode of exchange and coordination; socialism in these proposals describes ownership, governance, or the distribution of investment returns. Whether the combination is stable or desirable remains disputed.

commonQuestions.question: Is every worker cooperative an example of market socialism?
commonQuestions.answer: A cooperative can illustrate one institution associated with the tradition, but a firm operating inside a broader capitalist economy does not by itself establish a system-wide arrangement.

commonQuestions.question: Does market socialism eliminate competition?
commonQuestions.answer: Usually not. Many versions retain competition among enterprises while changing ownership and governance. Other versions limit markets in investment, land, essential services, or other domains.

traditions.caveat: Exploratory ideal-type description. It does not identify a country, case, advocate, or internally uniform tradition.

traditions.name: Central planning
traditions.description: state ownership and administrative allocation without market prices. Soviet-type; computational planning is the modern variant.
overview: Central planning is a family of arrangements that coordinates a substantial scope of production, investment, or distribution through collectively authorized plans and administrative or computational allocation. Ownership alone does not determine the mechanism: the revealing questions are who sets objectives, supplies information, revises targets, allocates resources, and contests decisions.

The family includes hierarchical administrative-command systems, indicative and mixed planning, and democratic or computational proposals. Historical command systems also operated through bargaining, managerial discretion, strategic reporting, and informal exchange; participatory computational designs may distribute operational authority differently. These are distinct institutional forms, not interchangeable evidence.
distinctions: Coordination rules, not state ownership alone
Economy-wide dominance is distinct from public investment or planning inside firms
Command, indicative, democratic, and computational forms should not be collapsed
A historical case is not the tradition itself

commonQuestions.question: Does central planning mean one office decides every detail?
commonQuestions.answer: Not necessarily. Plans can be hierarchical and distributed across agencies and enterprises. The analytical questions are which decisions are binding, where information moves, and who can correct errors.

commonQuestions.question: Is all public investment central planning?
commonQuestions.answer: No. Governments and firms routinely plan within market economies. This ideal type applies when administrative allocation replaces markets across a substantial range of production and investment decisions.

commonQuestions.question: Would better computers settle the planning debate?
commonQuestions.answer: Computation may change what can be processed, but it does not by itself settle how preferences are expressed, information is elicited, priorities are chosen, power is constrained, or errors are contested.

traditions.caveat: Exploratory ideal-type description. It does not identify a country, case, advocate, or internally uniform tradition.

traditions.name: Social anarchism
traditions.description: no state; production by federated worker associations or communes. Mutualism, collectivism, syndicalism, anarcho-communism. Spain 1936–39 is the main test; Ostrom's polycentric commons the closest documented small-scale analogue.
overview: Social anarchism groups traditions that reject the state and other entrenched hierarchies while emphasizing cooperation, mutual aid, common or worker control, and federated self-government. It includes mutualist, collectivist, anarcho-communist, and syndicalist currents that disagree over property, exchange, and organization.

Its institutional question is not whether organization disappears, but how coordination and enforcement might occur without a sovereign hierarchy. Proposals therefore focus on associations, councils, communes, unions, federations, and negotiated rules whose authority is intended to remain contestable from below.
distinctions: Opposition to hierarchy, not opposition to organization
Federation and association rather than an isolated localism
Several incompatible positions on markets, property, and remuneration

commonQuestions.question: Does anarchy mean the absence of rules?
commonQuestions.answer: Not in this tradition. Social anarchists typically distinguish rules and collective coordination from a state or entrenched hierarchy. The difficult issue is how rules gain legitimacy and are enforced without recreating domination.

commonQuestions.question: Is social anarchism necessarily anti-market?
commonQuestions.answer: No. Mutualist currents have defended forms of exchange and possession, while anarcho-communist currents reject markets more broadly. The category should preserve that disagreement.

commonQuestions.question: Does local self-government rule out large-scale coordination?
commonQuestions.answer: Not in theory. Federation is meant to connect local bodies across larger scales. Whether those arrangements can coordinate complex interdependence without concentrating authority is a central research question.

traditions.caveat: Exploratory ideal-type description. It does not identify a country, case, advocate, or internally uniform tradition.

traditions.name: State capitalism / developmental state
traditions.description: markets and private firms, with the state steering credit, protecting strategic sectors, and owning key enterprises. Singapore, South Korea, Taiwan; China since 1978.
overview: State capitalism and the developmental state are overlapping but contested labels for economies in which markets and firms operate alongside unusually directive public control over finance, investment, strategic sectors, or major enterprises. The state may act as owner, lender, coordinator, regulator, or partner to private capital.

The combined category is useful for exploring state direction, but it can also conceal important differences. Public ownership, authoritarian political control, export-oriented industrial policy, and ordinary regulation are not the same institution and should be separated in historical analysis.
distinctions: Market activity combined with directive state ownership or coordination
Developmental-state and state-capitalist labels overlap but are not synonyms
A contested analytical category rather than a neutral country classification

commonQuestions.question: Is every mixed economy state capitalist?
commonQuestions.answer: That usage would be too broad for this project. The category is most useful where state ownership, credit allocation, or strategic direction plays a defining role rather than merely setting background rules.

commonQuestions.question: Is a developmental state necessarily authoritarian?
commonQuestions.answer: No by definition, although prominent historical cases raise that association. Political regime, administrative capacity, industrial policy, and ownership should be modeled as related but separate dimensions.

commonQuestions.question: Does state ownership eliminate markets?
commonQuestions.answer: No. State-owned firms may sell in markets, compete, earn profits, and operate alongside private firms. Ownership and coordination mechanisms must be described separately.

traditions.caveat: Exploratory ideal-type description. It does not identify a country, case, advocate, or internally uniform tradition.

traditions.name: Anarcho-capitalism
traditions.description: no state; law, courts, and defense supplied by competing private agencies (Rothbard, David Friedman). No real-world case; medieval Iceland and Somalia 1991–2006 are the contested analogies.
overview: Anarcho-capitalism proposes extending private property, contract, and market competition to functions usually assigned to the state, including adjudication, policing, and defense. Its advocates imagine legal and protective services supplied by firms, associations, insurers, or other voluntary arrangements.

It shares market-liberal skepticism of public monopoly but differs by rejecting even the minimal state. The key institutional disputes concern whether rival protection agencies could remain competitive, how rights would be defined without a final public authority, and what meaningful consent requires under unequal bargaining power.
distinctions: No state, including no public monopoly on courts or defense
Distinct from minimal-state liberalism
A primarily theoretical tradition with disputed historical analogies

commonQuestions.question: Is anarcho-capitalism simply laissez-faire capitalism?
commonQuestions.answer: No. Laissez-faire positions commonly retain a minimal state. Anarcho-capitalism proposes private or associational substitutes for its courts, law enforcement, and defense functions.

commonQuestions.question: Does it mean that there would be no law?
commonQuestions.answer: Its advocates propose non-state legal rules and adjudication, not the absence of law. Critics question how conflicting rule systems would be reconciled and how coercive providers would be constrained.

commonQuestions.question: Are medieval Iceland or stateless Somalia proven examples?
commonQuestions.answer: No such classification should be treated as settled. They are contested analogies with institutional and historical differences that require bounded case analysis.

traditions.caveat: Exploratory ideal-type description. It does not identify a country, case, advocate, or internally uniform tradition.

traditions.name: Participatory economics (Parecon)
traditions.description: no markets, no state; worker and consumer councils, balanced job complexes, pay by effort, allocation by iterated participatory planning with indicative prices (Albert, Hahnel). No real-world case.
overview: Participatory economics, often called Parecon, is a specific proposal for coordinating production and consumption through worker and consumer councils rather than conventional markets or central command. Its design combines participatory planning, social ownership, balanced job complexes, and remuneration based on effort or sacrifice.

The model aims to distribute decision-making influence in proportion to how people are affected and to prevent both capitalist ownership and a managerial coordinator class. Its open questions concern information burdens, preference formation, expertise, incentives, and how iterative planning would work beyond models and small-scale exercises.
distinctions: A named institutional model rather than a broad family of all participatory practices
Council-based iterative planning rather than Soviet-style command planning
Balanced job complexes and effort-based remuneration are core, not optional details

commonQuestions.question: Is participatory economics another name for central planning?
commonQuestions.answer: No. It is designed around iterative proposals from worker and consumer councils rather than commands from a central authority. Critics may see related information problems, but the proposed decision structure is different.

commonQuestions.question: Does it retain ordinary markets?
commonQuestions.answer: The full model is intended to replace conventional markets for production and consumption with participatory planning and indicative prices. Partial adaptations may use some of its institutions without adopting the whole model.

commonQuestions.question: Has Parecon been implemented at national scale?
commonQuestions.answer: No national-scale implementation is established in this draft. Its large-scale performance therefore remains a theoretical and research question rather than an observed record.

traditions.caveat: Exploratory ideal-type description. It does not identify a country, case, advocate, or internally uniform tradition.

topics.label: Ownership
topics.description: Who may control productive assets, transfer them, and receive the gains or losses attached to them?

topics.label: Work
topics.description: How livelihood, authority, bargaining power, mobility, and security are organized around labor.

topics.label: Security
topics.description: How people and institutions respond to basic needs, shared risks, collective harms, and external threats.

topics.label: Coordination
topics.description: How information, resources, experimentation, and collective action are organized under uncertainty.

topics.label: Power
topics.description: Where consequential authority sits, how it changes, and how affected people can contest or constrain it.

challenges.question: How do participants learn what is needed and coordinate resources under dispersed, incomplete, or strategic information?
challenges.rationale: Coordination includes discovery, communication, calculation, and authority rather than presuming one allocation mechanism.

challenges.question: Who can initiate experiments, who bears their risks, and how does the arrangement learn from failure?
challenges.rationale: Innovation and failure are linked institutional problems involving permission, finance, loss, and adaptation.

challenges.question: Who captures gains from production, productivity, and ownership—and how can that distribution change?
challenges.rationale: Ownership, control, wages, profit, and wealth are distinct but interacting distributions.

challenges.question: Where does consequential authority sit, how can affected people contest it, and what limits capture or abuse?
challenges.rationale: Power can concentrate in workplaces, firms, associations, markets, or states; institutional safeguards should follow actual positions and powers.

challenges.question: How are diffuse harms, shared resources, and collective goods recognized, governed, and paid for?
challenges.rationale: The problem includes information, jurisdiction, enforcement, and distribution—not only whether prices exist.

challenges.question: Can people meaningfully leave firms, communities, or jurisdictions, and what dependencies shape that choice?
challenges.rationale: Formal exit is different from practical mobility when livelihood, care, geography, or membership constrain choice.

challenges.question: How are basic needs and protection against predictable life risks provided, and on what terms?
challenges.rationale: Provision must expose access, eligibility, financing, quality, discretion, and dependency.

challenges.question: How can institutions change from a specified starting point, and who bears the costs and risks of transition?
challenges.rationale: A transition is a path with actors, sequencing, resistance, and failure modes—not a property of an ideal endpoint.

challenges.question: How does an arrangement respond to external coercion without making emergency power permanently unaccountable?
challenges.rationale: Defense joins capacity against threats to the internal distribution and duration of coercive authority.

criteria.label: Distribution
criteria.definition: Who receives benefits, resources, authority, and adjustment costs?
normativeAssumptions: Concentrated advantages and involuntary burdens require explicit justification.
evidenceRequirements: Measures must distinguish income, wealth, ownership, control, access, and risk.
limitations: Improvement on one distribution does not establish improvement on another.

criteria.label: Accountability
criteria.definition: Can affected people inspect, contest, and replace consequential decision-makers?
normativeAssumptions: Consequential authority should be answerable to those it affects.
evidenceRequirements: Formal powers and observed practice must both be documented.
limitations: Formal contestability does not establish equal practical influence.

criteria.label: Scale and transferability
criteria.definition: Which contextual conditions are necessary for an observed mechanism to operate elsewhere or at another scale?
normativeAssumptions: No bounded case automatically supplies a universal blueprint.
evidenceRequirements: Compare population, jurisdiction, material conditions, participants, and rule levels.
limitations: Scale may change several mechanisms at once and cannot be reduced to population size.

failureHypotheses.text: The standard objection (Nozick): a successful agency becomes a state; an unsuccessful one loses to a state.

means.text: Councils submit consumption and production proposals; facilitation boards compute indicative prices; several rounds of revision converge on a plan.

failureHypotheses.text: Never tested. Critics (Schweickart, "Nonsense on Stilts") argue the iteration burden is enormous and indicative prices without real trades face the same calculation problem. Hahnel has only simulations.

means.text: Councils propose investments; workers are paid for effort, not output.

failureHypotheses.text: No risk-bearer; innovation is a collective proposal with no reward for success. Albert addresses this in a chapter; there is no evidence either way.

means.text: Social ownership; no wage labor; remuneration by effort and sacrifice, measured by co-workers.
Structural: no capital; balanced job complexes target the "coordinator class" — the technocratic elite that anarchism and Marxism both missed.

failureHypotheses.text: Effort is hard to measure and easy to game; balanced job complexes require rotating people out of tasks they are best at.
Untested; the coordinator-class analysis is Albert's most distinctive contribution and his answer to why Soviet planning produced a new elite.

means.text: Balanced job complexes: every worker does a mix of empowering and rote tasks so no "coordinator class" forms; councils decide.
No state; facilitation boards and councils.
Balanced job complexes and recallable councils prevent a coordinator class.

failureHypotheses.text: Its signature idea and its most criticized: rotating experts out of expert work trades competence for equality. Untested.
Untested; facilitation boards are the obvious capture target and the coordinator-class problem in miniature.
Designed against elite formation, not against coercion; unaddressed for armed or fraudulent actors.

means.text: Consumer councils weigh social and environmental impacts in the plan by construction.

failureHypotheses.text: Untested; depends on councils correctly valuing harms with no price benchmark.

means.text: Council membership; job complexes assigned within councils.

failureHypotheses.text: Movement between councils requires re-balancing job complexes; friction likely. Untested.

means.text: Consumption councils allocate by need within the plan.

failureHypotheses.text: Untested.

researchNotes.text: 19th-century Britain and U.S.; no modern pure case. Rapid growth alongside severe inequality and instability; every modern economy moved away from it.
Nordics since the 1930s; Germany since 1951; most of the OECD partially. Consistently high on freedom, health, mobility, innovation. Transferability contested.

Yugoslavia 1950–90; Mondragón since 1956; thousands of cooperatives. Co-ops match conventional productivity; Yugoslavia collapsed with its state; Mondragón reverts to capitalism abroad. No national case outlasting its regime.
USSR 1928–91; China 1949–78; Eastern bloc; Cuba; North Korea. Industrialization in priorities; shortage, stagnation, famine; every case liberalized or collapsed.
Spain 1936–39; Ukraine 1918–21; Rojava since 2012; Ostrom's commons; Zapatistas. Functional locally under wartime conditions; destroyed externally each time; no peacetime long-run test.

Japan 1950–90; Korea, Taiwan, Singapore since the 1960s; China since 1978. The strongest growth record of the last sixty years; Korea and Taiwan democratized, Singapore and China did not. The one system on this list whose track record is mostly positive and mostly recent.

No case. Medieval Iceland (930–1262) and Somalia 1991–2006 as contested analogies. Iceland's system ended in civil war and Norwegian rule; Somalia's outcome is disputed (Leeson vs. critics). No modern evidence.
No case. Small collectives (South End Press, Z Magazine). Nothing beyond a handful of workplaces.
Prices scale without limit; that is the point of the price mechanism. Public-goods and externality failures grow with scale (climate).
Scales via bureaucracy and law; the Nordics are 5–10 million each, Germany 84 million. Trust and homogeneity questions at U.S. or Indian scale; the largest social democracies are the most contested.
Individual cooperatives cap around 500 (Mondragón splits them); federations reach ~80,000. No national-scale case; the federation's own size bounds mobility and capital pooling.
Scales administratively — the USSR planned for 290 million. Information degrades with every layer of hierarchy; the calculation problem is a scale problem.
Strong at village, factory, and commons scale (Ostrom's cases are hundreds to thousands). Direct democracy and face-to-face trust do not survive scale; regional coordination in Spain was contested.
Scales to 1.4 billion (China) through state capacity. Local-government incentive distortion at scale (GDP-target gaming, debt); the center loses information the same way planners do.
Unknown; theory assumes competition among agencies at any scale. No evidence; agency competition at continental scale is speculation.
Planning rounds are combinatorial: every council's proposal affects every other's. The iteration burden grows faster than population; the strongest theoretical objection to the model.

sources.title: The Narrow Corridor (2019)
sources.note: **▶ Acemoglu & Robinson — *The Narrow Corridor* (2019).** The strong-state-vs-strong-society framing; built around exactly the two-sided fear of private and state concentration.

sources.title: Why Nations Fail (2012)
sources.note: **Acemoglu & Robinson — *Why Nations Fail* (2012).** Inclusive vs. extractive institutions; why some countries stay in the corridor.

sources.title: Federalist Nos
sources.note: **Madison — Federalist Nos. 10 and 51 (1787–88).** Short. Factions, and the original "ambition must be made to counteract ambition."

sources.title: Exit, Voice, and Loyalty (1970)
sources.note: **Hirschman — *Exit, Voice, and Loyalty* (1970).** Short. When exit disciplines power and when it just lets it escape.

sources.title: The Calculus of Consent (1962)
sources.note: **Buchanan & Tullock — *The Calculus of Consent* (1962).** Public choice: models officials as self-interested and asks which constitutional rules survive that assumption. The intellectual home of the government-tyranny worry.

sources.title: Governing the Commons (1990)
sources.note: **▶ Ostrom — *Governing the Commons* (1990).** Nobel-winning fieldwork on communities managing shared resources without privatization or central control.

sources.title: James C
sources.note: **▶ James C. Scott — *Seeing Like a State* (1998).** Why top-down "legibility" schemes fail; written by an anarchist-sympathetic political scientist, so it bridges to the anarchist section. Belongs equally under the calculation debate — it is about planning failure.

sources.title: Pillars of Prosperity (2011)
sources.note: **Besley & Persson — *Pillars of Prosperity* (2011).** State capacity as a development achievement; why weak states are often more predatory.

sources.title: The Theory of Economic Regulation (1971)
sources.note: **Stigler — "The Theory of Economic Regulation" (1971).** Short article. The foundational regulatory-capture argument.

sources.title: Varieties of Capitalism (2001)
sources.note: **Hall & Soskice (eds.) — *Varieties of Capitalism* (2001).** The "coordinated vs. liberal market economies" framework; the academic basis for treating Germany and the Nordics as a distinct system.

sources.title: The Road to Serfdom (1944) and Friedman — Capitalism and Freedom (1962)
sources.note: **Hayek — *The Road to Serfdom* (1944)** and **Friedman — *Capitalism and Freedom* (1962).** The canonical statements of the taxation-and-tyranny worry; the laissez-faire side of the argument.

sources.title: How China Became Capitalist (2012)
sources.note: **Coase & Wang — *How China Became Capitalist* (2012).** The state-capitalism / developmental-state case, from the author of "The Nature of the Firm."

sources.title: The Use of Knowledge in Society (1945)
sources.note: **▶ Hayek — "The Use of Knowledge in Society" (1945).** ~15 pages. The whole knowledge-problem argument.

sources.title: Economic Calculation in the Socialist Commonwealth (1920)
sources.note: **Mises — "Economic Calculation in the Socialist Commonwealth" (1920).** The original salvo.

sources.title: The Nature of the Firm (1937)
sources.note: **Coase — "The Nature of the Firm" (1937).** Short. Islands of planning in a sea of markets.

sources.title: The Socialist System (1992)
sources.note: **Kornai — *The Socialist System* (1992).** The soft-budget-constraint account from inside actually-existing planning.

sources.title: The Economics of Feasible Socialism (1983)
sources.note: **▶ Alec Nove — *The Economics of Feasible Socialism* (1983).** A socialist who took the calculation problem seriously and designed around it.

sources.title: Capitalism, Socialism, and Democracy (1942)
sources.note: **Schumpeter — *Capitalism, Socialism, and Democracy* (1942).** Creative destruction, plus an even-handed narration of the debate.

sources.title: The People's Republic of Walmart (2019)
sources.note: **Phillips & Rozworski — *The People's Republic of Walmart* (2019).** The modern pro-planning case built on corporate logistics.

sources.title: Towards a New Socialism (1993)
sources.note: **Cockshott & Cottrell — *Towards a New Socialism* (1993).** The computational-planning proposal.

sources.title: After Capitalism (2002)
sources.note: **▶ Schweickart — *After Capitalism* (2002).** The Economic Democracy model: worker self-management, markets for goods, socially controlled investment.

sources.title: Envisioning Real Utopias (2010)
sources.note: **▶ Erik Olin Wright — *Envisioning Real Utopias* (2010).** The best survey of real-world experiments (Mondragón, participatory budgeting, Wikipedia, basic income) with honest assessment of each.

sources.title: A Preface to Economic Democracy (1985)
sources.note: **Robert Dahl — *A Preface to Economic Democracy* (1985).** Short. The political-theory case that democratic principles apply to firms.

sources.title: Making Mondragon (1988)
sources.note: **Whyte & Whyte — *Making Mondragon* (1988).** The definitive institutional history; explains the capital-account mechanics.

sources.title: The Democratic Worker-Owned Firm (1990)
sources.note: **David Ellerman — *The Democratic Worker-Owned Firm* (1990).** The "labor theory of property" argument against the employment contract itself.

sources.title: Firms as Political Entities (2017)
sources.note: **Isabelle Ferreras — *Firms as Political Entities* (2017).** "Economic bicameralism": a workers' chamber alongside the shareholders' chamber. The most developed extension of codetermination.

sources.title: A Future for Socialism (1994)
sources.note: **John Roemer — *A Future for Socialism* (1994).** A different market-socialist design (coupon-based shares), for contrast with Schweickart.

sources.title: Parecon: Life After Capitalism (2003)
sources.note: **Michael Albert — *Parecon: Life After Capitalism* (2003).** Participatory economics; the main non-market democratic proposal. (Albert is sole author; Hahnel co-wrote the earlier academic statements, *The Political Economy of Participatory Economics* and *Looking Forward*, both 1991.) Pair with Schweickart's 2006 critique, "Nonsense on Stilts: Michael Albert's Parecon" — a direct market-socialist vs. non-market exchange.

sources.title: The Citizen's Share (2013)
sources.note: **Blasi, Freeman & Kruse — *The Citizen's Share* (2013).** Empirical record of employee ownership in the U.S.

sources.title: Democracy at Work (2012)
sources.note: **Richard Wolff — *Democracy at Work* (2012).** Accessible; worker self-directed enterprises.

sources.title: What Does Codetermination Do? (NBER Working Paper 28921, 2021)
sources.note: **Jäger & Noy — "What Does Codetermination Do?" (NBER Working Paper 28921, 2021).** The empirical basis for the codetermination claims in Part 1.

sources.title: What do we really know about worker co-operatives? (Co-operatives UK, 2016)
sources.note: **Pérotin — "What do we really know about worker co-operatives?" (Co-operatives UK, 2016).** The productivity meta-review cited in Part 1.

sources.title: The Institutional Foundations of Middle-Class Democracy (Policy Network, 2011)
sources.note: **Hacker — "The Institutional Foundations of Middle-Class Democracy" (Policy Network, 2011).** Where "predistribution" was coined.

sources.title: What Is Property? (1840)
sources.note: **Proudhon — *What Is Property?* (1840).** The mutualist foundation; possession vs. property.

sources.title: The Conquest of Bread (1892) and Mutual Aid (1902)
sources.note: **Kropotkin — *The Conquest of Bread* (1892) and *Mutual Aid* (1902).** Anarcho-communism; *Mutual Aid* argues cooperation, not just competition, drives evolution and social order — it supports the anarchist premise rather than describing the system.

sources.title: Statism and Anarchy (1873)
sources.note: **Bakunin — *Statism and Anarchy* (1873).** The collectivist critique of Marx, including the prediction that a "workers' state" becomes a new ruling class.

sources.title: Anarcho-Syndicalism: Theory and Practice (1938)
sources.note: **Rudolf Rocker — *Anarcho-Syndicalism: Theory and Practice* (1938).** The standard statement.

sources.title: Anarchy in Action (1973)
sources.note: **▶ Colin Ward — *Anarchy in Action* (1973).** Short, practical; treats anarchism as already present in how people organize. Good fit for an engineering mindset.

sources.title: James C
sources.note: **James C. Scott — *Two Cheers for Anarchism* (2012).** Short essays; the "two cheers" hedge is honest about limits.

sources.title: Organization Theory: A Libertarian Perspective (2008)
sources.note: **▶ Kevin Carson — *Organization Theory: A Libertarian Perspective* (2008).** A mutualist applying the Coase firm-size question to argue that state intervention subsidizes firms beyond their efficient scale. Directly relevant to the concentration thread. *Note:* self-published (BookSurge, Center for a Stateless Society) by an independent scholar — a serious argument, not a peer-reviewed authority.

sources.title: The Anarchist Collectives (1974)
sources.note: **Sam Dolgoff (ed.) — *The Anarchist Collectives* (1974).** Primary documents from Spain 1936–39, the only large-scale test.

sources.title: The Next Revolution (2015)
sources.note: **Murray Bookchin — *The Next Revolution* (2015).** Libertarian municipalism; the theoretical basis for Rojava's confederalism. *Note:* Bookchin broke with anarchism in 1999 and called his later politics "Communalism"; this posthumous collection is mostly post-break essays. Adjacent to anarchism rather than inside it.

sources.title: The Dawn of Everything (2021)
sources.note: **Graeber & Wengrow — *The Dawn of Everything* (2021).** Argues the archaeological record shows far more variety in political organization than "state or chaos" allows. Anthropology by anarchists, not anarchist theory — background, not a statement of the tradition.

sources.title: The Government of No One (2019)
sources.note: **Ruth Kinna — *The Government of No One* (2019).** A modern scholarly map of the tradition before diving into primary sources.

sources.title: Capital in the Twenty-First Century (2014)
sources.note: **Piketty — *Capital in the Twenty-First Century* (2014).** The r > g argument for why concentration is the default.

sources.title: The Curse of Bigness (2018)
sources.note: **▶ Tim Wu — *The Curse of Bigness* (2018).** Short. The neo-Brandeisian case that concentration is a political problem, not just a price problem.

sources.title: Amazon's Antitrust Paradox (2017, Yale Law Journal)
sources.note: **Lina Khan — "Amazon's Antitrust Paradox" (2017, *Yale Law Journal*).** The article that relaunched the antitrust debate.

sources.title: Progress and Poverty (1879)
sources.note: **Henry George — *Progress and Poverty* (1879).** The land-value-tax argument; the core is in the first third.

sources.title: The Stakeholder Society (1999)
sources.note: **Ackerman & Alstott — *The Stakeholder Society* (1999).** Universal basic capital.

sources.title: Republic, Lost (2011)
sources.note: **Lessig — *Republic, Lost* (2011).** Money in politics as systemic rather than individual corruption.

sources.title: Open Democracy (2020)
sources.note: **Landemore — *Open Democracy* (2020).** The strongest case for sortition and citizens' assemblies as capture-resistant institutions.
